title: Plan-and-execute
summary: A planner writes the steps first, then an executor carries them out, often with cheaper calls and without reasoning after every tool result. A replan step handles surprises.
useIf: Tool chains are fairly predictable, you want a reviewable plan before side effects, or token cost per run matters more than step-by-step flexibility.
avoidIf: Each tool result changes what you should do next, or the environment shifts faster than a plan can stay valid.

explain.md: **Plan-and-execute** splits thinking from doing. A planner produces an ordered list of steps; an executor runs them, usually one tool call or small subtask at a time; a replanner revises the remaining steps if a step fails or reveals new facts. Plan-and-Solve prompting was introduced to reduce the missing-step errors of zero-shot chain of thought by devising a plan first and then executing the subtasks [[r38]]. ReWOO goes further by decoupling reasoning from tool observations, so the plan can reference earlier results by placeholder and tools run without a model call between them. It reports 5x token efficiency and 4 percent higher accuracy on HotpotQA against interleaved reasoning [[r18]].

explain.title: Plan, execute, replan
explain.alt: A planner writes a plan, an executor runs each step, a check decides whether to continue, replan or finish.
explain.src:
flowchart LR
  P[Planner: write steps] --> E[Executor: run next step]
  E --> C{Result as expected?}
  C -->|yes, more steps| E
  C -->|surprise| R[Replan remaining steps]
  R --> E
  C -->|done| F[Final answer]

explain.md: The plan is also an artifact. You can show it to a user, store it, diff it and require approval before anything runs. Magentic orchestration in Microsoft Agent Framework builds on this idea with a task ledger and a flag for human review of the plan [[r10]]. The weakness is brittleness: a plan written before the first observation encodes assumptions that may be wrong, and a long plan executed blindly compounds a bad assumption. Replanning on failure, and short plans for uncertain tasks, are the usual defences.

explain.title: Reasoning models blur the line
explain.md: OpenAI advises giving reasoning models a clear goal, constraints and an output contract instead of scripting every step [[r34]]. A strong reasoning model may plan internally. An explicit plan still helps when you need approval, audit or cheaper executors.

whereToUse: Multi-step API or data tasks with stable tool chains
Tasks that need a plan reviewed before any write or spend
Long jobs where a small model can execute steps a larger model planned
Reports and analyses that follow a known outline
Agents where token cost matters and tool results are small and checkable

use: Steps and tools are predictable enough to plan
Someone needs to see or approve the plan first
Execution steps are simple enough for a cheaper model
avoid: Early observations usually overturn the plan
The task is short enough that a plan is more tokens than the work
flips: Replans happen on most runs: switch to ReAct
Plans repeat across runs: freeze them as a workflow
Steps need judgement mid-way: let the executor reason, not only call tools

pitfalls.symptom: Step four fails because step two returned something the plan did not expect
pitfalls.cause: The plan assumed a result shape before seeing it
pitfalls.fix: Validate each step's result, replan the remainder on mismatch, and keep plans short for uncertain tasks.

pitfalls.symptom: The executor follows the plan after the goal has changed
pitfalls.cause: No replan trigger when the user or the facts change
pitfalls.fix: Check the plan against new input at each step boundary and replan on conflict.

pitfalls.symptom: Planning costs more than the work
pitfalls.cause: A large model writes a long plan for a three-call task
pitfalls.fix: Skip planning for short tasks, or use a small model with a template for the plan.

scenarios.title: Stable chain, cost pressure
scenarios.situation: A nightly job reconciles records across four internal systems. The tool order is nearly always the same, tool results are small, and the bill is the concern.
unknowns: How often does a step return something unexpected?
scenarios.question: Which loop shape do you choose?

options.name: Plan-and-execute with a cheap executor and replan on mismatch
options.why: Stable chains benefit from planning once and running cheaply. The replan path covers rare surprises.
options.tradeoff: More engineering than a simple loop, and the plan needs validation.

options.name: Plain ReAct on a large model
options.tradeoff: Pays for reasoning after every tool result when the chain rarely changes.

options.name: One huge prompt that does all four systems in one call
options.why: Tool calls still need executing, and one call cannot react to a failed step.
options.tradeoff: Fine only for tasks with no tools, where one call can do the work.

flips.if: Reconciliation steps vary a lot per record

flips.then: Replace the planner with a workflow in code.

scenarios.takeaway: Plan once when the world is stable. Replan only when it is not.

scenarios.title: Review before side effects
scenarios.situation: An agent will provision resources and send messages on a user's behalf. The user wants to see what it intends to do before anything happens. Runs are low volume.
constraints: Side effects cannot all be undone
unknowns: Can the plan be shown in a readable form?
What happens if the user edits a step?
scenarios.question: How do you structure the run?

options.name: Generate a plan, require approval, execute steps with checks and replan on failure
options.why: The plan is a reviewable artifact and approval happens before any side effect.
options.tradeoff: Added user friction and a plan that may need editing.

options.name: ReAct loop with an approval prompt on each write
options.why: Gates only the risky calls and adapts to results.
options.tradeoff: Many interruptions, and the user never sees the whole intent up front.

options.name: Autonomous loop with logging only
options.why: Logs help after the fact but cannot undo messages already sent.
options.tradeoff: Right for read-only tasks or fully reversible actions.

flips.then: Drop plan approval and rely on audit and compensation.
Persist the plan and run state durably so the wait costs nothing.

scenarios.takeaway: A plan is the cheapest place to put a human.

quiz.q: What does ReWOO change compared with an interleaved reasoning loop?
options: It decouples reasoning from tool observations, so tool calls run without a model call between them
It removes tools from the agent
It trains the model on each tool
It runs all steps in parallel
quiz.explain: ReWOO plans with placeholders for tool results and runs tools without interleaved reasoning, reporting 5x token efficiency and 4 percent higher accuracy on HotpotQA. It still uses tools and is not inherently parallel. [[r18]]

quiz.q: Replans occur on 70 percent of runs. What is the sensible change?
options: Move toward a ReAct loop, since observations are steering the work
quiz.explain: Frequent replans show observations change the path, which is the ReAct case. Longer plans bake in more wrong assumptions, disabling replanning breaks failure handling and a second planner adds cost.

flashcards.front: What is the main weakness of plan-and-execute?
flashcards.back: Brittleness. A plan written before the first observation can rest on wrong assumptions, so you need replanning and short plans for uncertain tasks.
5x token efficiency and 4 percent higher accuracy on HotpotQA versus interleaved reasoning, by decoupling reasoning from tool observations [[r18]].

flashcards.front: Why is a plan useful beyond cost?
flashcards.back: It is an artifact you can show, store, diff and approve before side effects run.
